ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The transition to neighborhood-scale district heating in the Netherlands frequently stalls due to the challenge of achieving a collective agreement among individual homeowners. To explore the micro-dynamics of this collective action problem, this paper introduces an agent-based model that integrates three key drivers of collective choice: heterogeneous decision styles (deliberative, social-comparison, repetition, imitation), networked social pressure governed by bounded confidence and minority influence, and dynamic information diffusion with spatiotemporal decay. A novel three-layer architecture maps the progression from continuous opinion exchange to voting intention and a final binary vote. Scenario experiments reveal the system's fragility and key leverage points: the benchmark scenario, which targets community leaders with early positive information, achieves an 88 % yes-vote share, while early endorsement by cross-cutting brokers who link different sub-communities achieves a 97 % yes-vote share and high agreement (0.866 global consensus; 1 indicates unanimity). Conversely, a single, early negative narrative can trigger a rapid collapse of support from over 90 % households within 30 simulation rounds. Late-stage positive messages proved most efficient at tipping fence-sitters, achieving 95 % yes votes with smaller aggregate opinion shifts than early messaging. A comparative analysis across small-world, scale-free, and random networks demonstrates that these mechanisms are robust. These findings indicate that information timing, targeting, and valence serve as critical non-economic levers in community energy transition, and yield actionable heuristics for policy: target credible brokers such as local energy coaches with data-rich information early, use visible social proof just before a decision point, and actively neutralize negative narratives to prevent cascading resistance.

ce:section.ce:para: Climate change mitigation demands a rapid transformation of the way societies produce and consume energy. The residential sector accounts for approximately 40 % of final energy demand, and over one-third of direct carbon emissions are from buildings in the European Union [1]. Decarbonizing this sector is one of the flagship objectives of the Union's “Fit for 55” policy package, which calls for a 55 % reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 and net-zero emissions by 2050 [2]. In the Netherlands, the Dutch Climate Agreement aims to phase out gas use entirely in the built environment by mid-century [3]. As local authorities accelerate plans to disconnect whole neighborhoods from the gas grid, neighborhood-level ballots have become a bottleneck of heat decarbonization, because installing a district-heating grid, or any shared alternative to a gas boiler, requires a collective “all-in” commitment, not a single-household swap.

Low-carbon heating options such as district-heating networks, shared geothermal wells, or clustered all-electric heat pump plants exhibit strong economies of scale. The pipes are an indivisible public good: everyone on the network benefits once it is built, but the high sunk cost must be financed first. Households, therefore, face a threshold-public-goods dilemma: each prefers the system to be built but hopes others will commit first, especially when early adopters face higher perceived risks [4]. Consequently, such projects require a super-majority vote before funding construction, making community persuasion as critical as engineering design or tariff modeling [5].

Empirical studies in energy transition indicate that peer effects and social influence can significantly affect technology adoption rates [6–8]. This implies that a binding vote is not merely an aggregation of private preferences, but the endpoint of an inherently social process of opinion formation, one that is difficult to capture with models that abstract away interaction.

Yet two gaps limit prevailing modeling approaches. First, classic diffusion-of-innovation theory and energy-economy models often assume homogeneous adopters or representative agents, which fail to capture the diversity of decision-making behaviors [9–11]. In reality, communities consist of individuals with diverse cognitive styles and susceptibilities to social influence. Some people are deliberative and weigh evidence carefully; others are more prone to follow social trends or trusted peers. Some remain confident in their initial convictions despite contrary information, whereas others readily adjust their views under peer pressure. Such heterogeneity can yield collective trajectories that homogeneous models miss [12].

The second gap concerns the opinion-to-action pathway. Bounded confidence models trace how continuous opinions cluster or polarize [13–15], but stop before the decisive act (e.g., a ‘yes’ vote). Conversely, diffusion models in energy technology adoption often jump directly to who adopts or not, without modeling the nuanced opinion formation process leading to that choice. Bridging these levels calls for an integrated framework that maps evolving attitudes onto discrete collective choices under realistic social influence.

To address these gaps, this paper develops an agent-based model (ABM) which integrates (i) heterogeneous decision styles, (ii) bounded confidence opinion exchange with minority resistance, and (iii) spatiotemporal information decay, and ties them in a three-layer loop that mirrors real deliberation-intention-ballot cycles.

This model contributes to a growing ABM literature on energy transition. Within community energy systems (CES), ABMs serve purposes ranging from predicting technology diffusion to explaining why some initiatives succeed, and much of this work has focused on electricity generation and has often been grounded in economic or institutional theories [16].

One major stream of ABM research models technology adoption and diffusion. These models often explore how factors like subsidies, information campaigns, and social networks influence the uptake of technologies like PV panels or heat pumps. For instance, Nava-Guerrero et al. [17] developed an ABM to explore the adoption of competing heating technologies based on households’ multi-criteria preferences, while their earlier work explored the role of group decisions in homeowner associations [8].

Another significant stream focuses on the formation and governance of energy communities, often drawing on institutional theories. Models [18–20] utilize frameworks like Ostrom's Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework and Social Value Orientation (SVO) to explore how leadership, trust, and institutional rules enable or constrain the emergence of successful energy communities.

While this body of work provides a rich understanding of policy impacts and institutional design, comparatively less attention has been paid to the micro-level social-psychological dynamics through which discussion, persuasion, and resistance translate into a binding ballot outcome. This study explicitly models these pre-decisional dynamics, distinguishing it from ABMs that focus primarily on adoption outcomes or institutional conditions.

The epistemological purpose of this model, following the taxonomy of modeling purposes in computational social science [21], is a theoretical exploration rather than an empirical prediction (which typically forecasts technology diffusion). Its primary goal is not to replicate a specific real-world case with quantitative accuracy, but to serve as a computational sandbox for examining the emergent, collective outcomes that arise from the interaction of well-established social-psychological theories: bounded confidence, social impact, and dual-process cognition. By formalizing these mechanisms and their interplay, the model could rigorously explore “what-if” scenarios and generate hypotheses about the dynamics of collective choice that would be difficult to derive from verbal theory alone [22]. The policy guidance derived is therefore strategic and heuristic, aimed at identifying key sensitivities and leverage points, rather than providing a prescriptive blueprint.

While the specific parameterization is for district heating, the underlying framework for modeling opinion-to-action pathways offers insights applicable to other collective choice problems where timing, targeting, and framing of information steer outcomes. The model is applied in a voting scenario where community members engage in multiple rounds of discussion, receive information, and only then make a final vote (in this paper, adoption denotes the yes-vote share in the final ballot). Specifically, this paper makes the following methodological contributions to the exploration of collective action in energy transition:i.
Exploring the emergent consequences of cognitive heterogeneity by integrating four decision styles (deliberative, social-comparison, repetition, imitation) drawn from empirical studies within a small-world network.ii.
Investigating the theoretical impact of social filtering on opinion dynamics by operationalizing bounded confidence theory as a mechanism for networked social pressure and minority resistance.iii.
Examining the system-level effects of information propagation through a dynamic diffusion process with spatial-temporal decay, where information is targeted at emergent community leaders.iv.
Proposing a novel three-layer agent architecture that maps the progression from continuous internal opinion dynamics to a final, discrete collective voting outcome, bridging a common gap between opinion models and adoption models.

These model features raise two key questions about collective voting. First: How does neighborhood community structure amplify or dampen collective commitment? Second: How do the timing, targeting, and framing of information campaigns interact with that structure to make a heat transition stall or scale up?

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 details the empirical and theoretical building blocks; Section 3 describes the three-layer agent-based model; Section 4 verifies the model's credibility; Section 5 presents the scenario design and simulation results, and addresses the questions posed above; Section 6 concludes the paper and suggests directions for future research.

Opinion dynamics research and energy-system modeling increasingly face a common challenge: how to link micro-level cognition to macro-level adoption while still reflecting household-specific circumstances? Agent-based models (ABMs) offer that bridge. By encoding psychological rules in artificial households and letting them interact on an explicit social network, ABMs reveal neighborhood-scale patterns that are difficult to represent in cost-optimization models [9], and are widely used in the residential energy context: district heating transition, heat pump diffusion, solar panel uptake, and EV-charger siting [23–25].

Understanding these transition decisions requires integrating diverse perspectives from economics, psychology, and sociology [26]. These interdisciplinary insights reveal that household decisions exist on a spectrum from impulsive to deliberative, with no single theoretical paradigm fully capturing this complexity. Therefore, this research draws on multiple social-scientific theories to model collective decision-making about a collective heat-transition vote in a computational agent-based framework (Fig. 1). In Fig. 1, blue boxes denote the theories; yellow boxes show the model components derived from them; green boxes mark the three simulation layers (opinion-intention-vote).

Together, these theories supply compatible building blocks for the ABM: bounded confidence selects interaction partners, Social Impact Theory scales their influence, dual-process cognition weights incoming signals by agent type, and information diffusion feeds those signals through the network with spatial and temporal decay.

Field evidence motivates this design. Dutch neighborhood pilots show that super-majority consent rules either delay or accelerate heat transitions depending on which residents (leaders or late-movers) change their mind first [8]. Diffusion studies further quantify peer effects: the probability that a household adopts a low-carbon technology can increase substantially once salient neighbors have done so [27,28]. These data justify modeling (i) detailed social topology and (ii) heterogeneous decision styles, because both shape who persuades whom and how fast agreement forms.

By embedding all these elements in an agent-based model, an integrative framework is created to examine how micro-level cognition and social interactions produce emergent collective outcomes in energy behavior [29]. The subsections below describe each theoretical component and its role in the model.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Bounded confidence theory in opinion dynamics
ce:section.ce:para: Bounded confidence theory [13] explains how opinion convergence is limited by individuals' willingness to consider only similar viewpoints. In this classic Hegselmann-Krause model, agents adjust their opinions by averaging those of their neighbors, but only if the neighbor's opinion lies within a certain tolerance range (the “confidence bound”). In other words, each agent interacts only with others holding opinions not too far from their own, reflecting a form of selective exposure or bounded rationality in social judgment. This mechanism can lead to distinct group outcomes: if the confidence bound is narrow, clusters of like-minded agents persist (potentially yielding polarized subgroups or fragmented consensus), whereas a sufficiently broad bound allows opinions to coalesce into overall agreement. Bounded confidence thus offers a theoretical basis for understanding how consensus, polarization, or persistent dissent might emerge from iterative interpersonal exchanges.

Relative agreement [11] extends bounded confidence by replacing the binary influence rule with graded influence based on overlap: when two agents interact, the strength of influence is proportional to the overlap of their opinion intervals. If the intervals barely overlap, agents influence each other weakly; if the intervals fully overlap, the interaction approaches the maximal update of the original Deffuant rule. Thus, relative agreement extends bounded confidence by turning the sharp ϵ cutoff into a continuous weighting scheme, preserving the intuition of limited receptivity while avoiding unrealistic discontinuities. In energy contexts, e.g., deliberations on adopting district heating systems, this refinement captures the empirical observation that homeowners are more persuaded by nearby opinions yet remain somewhat responsive to moderately different views rather than switching off influence entirely.

Within the simulation, bounded confidence serves as the prerequisite for interaction: an agent is influenced only by neighbors whose current opinions lie inside a predetermined threshold. This rule reproduces the tendency to dismiss information deemed “too extreme” and leads to cluster formation, with consensus emerging only under sufficiently broad confidence bounds: an outcome consistent with observed splits between early adopters and skeptics in residential energy transition.

The magnitude of each update is further scaled by the relative-agreement coefficient, producing a hybrid mechanism that preserves cluster formation while delivering graded convergence rates and, consequently, a nuanced spectrum from consensus to stalemate.

Human decision-making is profoundly shaped by social influence processes, both majority and minority pressures. The majority influence pressures individuals to conform to prevalent norms or opinions, and Social-Impact Theory formalizes how this pressure depends on the strength, immediacy, and number of influencing others (sources) relative to the target individual [30,31]. In essence, an individual is more likely to change their stance if many close and credible peers advocate a certain position. This reflects everyday observations: for instance, a homeowner may feel swayed to invest in energy-efficient appliances if most of their neighbors (and especially those whose opinions they value) have done so. Social-Impact Theory provides the model with a quantitative rationale for modeling interpersonal influence: each agent's susceptibility to change is a function of the proportion and persuasiveness of its informed neighbors [32–34].

Minority influence, in turn, shows that a consistent and confident minority can trigger private attitude change within the majority [35]. In community energy settings, a handful of “green champions” may gradually convert skeptics through persistent advocacy. The model, therefore, assigns a subset of agents unwavering convictions; repeated exposure to these agents can create tipping points at which the minority view diffuses network-wide.

At each simulation step, the influence from neighbors is weighted by their number and strength, reflecting both density and credibility. An agent embedded among numerous proponents of an energy-saving technology therefore experiences stronger social pressure than one with only sparse advocates. A designated subset of “stubborn” or “leader” agents introduces persistent minority pressure, allowing the model to explore scenarios where consistent dissent either blocks consensus or reverses majority views. The interaction between majority pressure and minority resistance thus produces realistic tensions between conformity and innovation.

Although bounded confidence mechanisms highlight homophily, conformity pressure can counteract fragmentation. Experiments in the Asch tradition show that moderate group pressure often restores consensus despite initial divergence. Hybrid models that couple bounded confidence with social pressure demonstrate that when individuals are swayed by a sufficiently large local majority, the population tends to reach consensus more often than in the standard bounded-confidence scenario [36–38].

An individual's decision-making process can follow different cognitive pathways. Modeling this cognitive heterogeneity is a central challenge in energy transition, and various theoretical frameworks have been employed for this purpose. For instance, the Social Value Orientation (SVO) theory [39] classifies individuals based on their pro-social versus pro-self motivations (e.g., cooperative, individualistic) and has been used to model motivations for joining thermal energy communities [40]. Another approach is the Capability Approach [41], which assesses how different individuals convert resources into well-being, highlighting potential value conflicts and justice issues in decarbonization [42].

For this model, which focuses on the dynamics of information processing and opinion change, Dual-process theories distinguish between a fast, heuristic mode of thinking (often called System 1 or intuitive processing) and a slow, deliberative mode (System 2 or analytical reasoning). This duality implies that a population will be heterogeneous: some actors rely more on gut feelings or social cues, while others systematically weigh costs and benefits. The Consumat framework [43] for consumer behavior modeling, for instance, classifies agents into modes like repetition, imitation, inquiring, and optimizing depending on their needs and uncertainty.

Agent heterogeneity is represented through four decision-making styles that map onto the dual-process distinction. High-heuristic agents alter behavior based on simple cues (“a neighbor installed LED lighting, therefore the upgrade is appealing”), whereas deliberative agents revise opinions only after evaluating evidence such as payback periods or risk profiles. Including both extremes reproduces real-world diversity, where some households follow trends and others demand analytic justification.

The framework now creates a synergistic chain of mechanisms by integrating this dual-process theory with others. Bounded confidence theory serves as the initial social filter, determining if an agent is receptive to a neighbor's opinion. Social Impact Theory then quantifies the magnitude of conformity pressure exerted by the local majority. Finally, the dual-process formulation governs how an agent internally weighs these social signals against exogenous information and its own beliefs. This integration could model the complete pathway from signal reception to cognitive processing to opinion update, capturing a dynamic interplay that a single theoretical lens would miss.

Collective outcomes depend not only on static peer influence but also on time-dependent Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) [44–46]. In many social systems, individuals receive information about innovations, policies, or behaviors through their network connections (friends, family, media, etc.), which in turn affects their choices. Classic diffusion of innovations theory posits that awareness and adoption spread via interpersonal contacts in a roughly S-shaped curve as early adopters inform others and social proof accumulates. Dynamic diffusion is represented by injecting news into a subset of seed agents and permitting stepwise propagation. For instance, a government heat pump rebate can originate with well-connected residents and spread through neighborhood contacts, progressively altering attitudes.

At each step, every uninformed agent receives information from informed neighbors with a probability that decays in space and time [47,48]. The resulting decision environment is therefore endogenous and time-varying. Diffusion interacts with bounded confidence and social-impact pressure: a persuasive message that rapidly attains critical mass can trigger a conformity cascade, whereas strict confidence bounds confine the message to receptive clusters. This design enables the reproduction of observed lags, cascades, and heterogeneous rollout speeds in energy technology adoption without assuming universal information access.

In this model, each theoretical component contributes a layer of realism to the simulation of energy-related collective decisions. The bounded confidence rule sets the social topology of influence by controlling who listens to whom, while social impact and minority influence theories govern how strongly agents sway each other in that topology. Dual-process heterogeneity ensures that agents differ in responsiveness and decision criteria, reflecting the mix of habit and deliberation in real communities. Dynamic diffusion injects an evolving information context that agents react to over time. In sum, the theoretical framework provides a coherent basis for modeling how individual cognitive processes and social influences jointly shape collective decisions in energy systems, bridging insights from behavioral theory and social network dynamics in a manner suitable for computational analysis.

Building on the above theoretical foundations, an agent-based model (ABM) is developed. A three-layer opinion formation process connects individual-level dynamics to voting intentions, which in turn aggregate into a collective decision. Each agent possesses attributes such as an initial opinion and a decision-making style, and interacts with neighboring agents under bounded confidence principles. A key feature of this model is its ability to represent how information propagates through dynamically evolving social structures. Unlike models with static social networks, this model assumes that influence clusters, or communities, are not fixed but emerge and shift as opinions evolve. Every τ steps, communities are re-identified with the Louvain algorithm [51], which is a widely used heuristic for optimizing network modularity, chosen here for its computational efficiency and scalability, which makes it suitable for repeated application within a simulation run. Within each community, a leader set is defined as the top-q% highest composite centrality nodes (degree + betweenness + eigenvector), who are the primary recipients of exogenous information shocks. This creates a feedback loop: micro-level opinion shifts create macro-level community structures, which in turn shape the subsequent flow of information. This approach offers a complementary perspective to other ABMs of energy communities. For example, some models [19,20,40] often conceptualize groups and their decision-making based on pre-defined institutional frameworks or agent typologies. This model, in contrast, does not pre-suppose these structures but rather explores how they might endogenously emerge from the fundamental dynamics of social influence, providing insights into the pre-institutional phase of consensus formation.

Each simulation experiment is run for a total of T=150 rounds. The simulation begins at t=0 with the initialization of the agent population and network structure, terminates when t=T if early stopping mechanism is not triggered, at which point the final voting is conducted and headline metrics are recorded. A simulation round does not correspond to a fixed unit of real-world time (e.g., a day or a month). Instead, it represents a single discrete time step in which a randomly selected pair of connected agents has the opportunity to interact and potentially update their opinions.

To ensure the results were robust against stochasticity, the necessary number of simulation replicates was determined. Convergence analysis of the mean and standard deviation of key output variables (e.g., final yes-rate rate) indicates stabilization after approximately 300–400 runs. Therefore, 500 independent Monte-Carlo runs were conducted, consistent with practices for mitigating aleatory uncertainty in complex ABMs [52]. The first test then examined emergent social patterns across these runs (Table 5).

All 40 simulated neighborhoods reached stable opinions, confirming numerical convergence of the three-layer architecture. A herding frequency of 80 % mirrors empirical evidence that social learning produces geographically clustered uptake in community energy transition (e.g., the spatial diffusion of residential PV documented by Ref. [53]). An echo chamber prevalence of 32.5 % reflects the partial information segregation observed in real networks, in which some communities develop distinct narratives yet retain links to wider information flows. Together, these outcomes indicate that the model reproduces key social-influence mechanisms, convergence, bandwagoning, and local segregation, without generating unrealistically high polarization.

Robustness against stochastic variation was assessed by repeating each scenario 200 times with different random seeds. For every run, the four headline indicators, final adoption rate, mean opinion, opinion standard deviation, and global consensus, were recorded; 10000 bootstrap resamples (bias-corrected, 95 % level) then yielded the confidence intervals reported in Table 6. All coefficients of variation (standard deviation divided by mean) are below 0.10, and the narrow percentile ranges (e.g., adoption 0.656–0.944) show that dispersion remains moderate relative to the mean. These findings confirm that outcome variability is driven mainly by systematic parameter settings rather than by random noise, validating the model's suitability for policy-oriented scenario exploration.

A comprehensive sensitivity analysis was undertaken to assess internal validity and computational robustness. Following best practices for complex ABMs, the analysis proceeded in multiple stages and four computational performance aspects (efficiency, convergence, reliability, and robustness) were evaluated [54–56].

Given the large number of parameters in the model (see Tables 3 and 4), an exhaustive exploration of all interactions was computationally infeasible. Instead, an initial screening identified the most influential parameters driving the primary outcome (final yes-vote share), and then a two-stage sensitivity study was conducted. First, a global exploration was performed with 50 Latin-hypercube draws across behaviorally salient parameters. Second, a focused One-at-a-Time (OFAT) analysis examined the parameters with higher importance scores to gain deeper insights into their effects.

All model parameters governing agent interaction, decision-making, and information flow were considered during the screening. Through a series of preliminary exploratory runs (analogous to an Elementary Effects test), the relative impact of each parameter on the final adoption rate was assessed. This screening process revealed that while nearly all parameters affect model dynamics to some degree, the variance in the primary outcome was overwhelmingly driven by a subset of seven parameters that control the core dynamic processes of learning, social influence, and information decay. In contrast, parameters representing static thresholds (e.g. θv, sthre) exhibited more predictable, linear effects and were thus held at their baseline values to focus the analysis on key non-linear dynamics. The seven parameters selected for in-depth analysis were: trust_adjustment_rate (ψ), info_decay_rate (λ), learning_rate (μbase), minority_resistance (rm), memory_decay (δ), conformity_strength (γc), direct_opinion_impact (ξ).

Fig. 4 visualizes four orthogonal importance estimators: random-forest Gini, permutation drop-out, standardized linear coefficients, and Spearman correlation [57–59], and combined into an averaged consensus score (dotted line).

The stability of this ranking across methods is particularly noteworthy given the different theoretical foundations of each approach: random forests capture non-linear relationships and interactions, permutation addresses feature importance through prediction degradation, linear coefficients assess direct linear effects, and Spearman correlation captures monotonic relationships without linearity assumptions. This multi-method convergence provides strong evidence for the robustness of the importance assessment.

Relational dynamics are dominant: the three top parameters regulate how rapidly agents react to one another through edge-weight updates, exogenous-cue propagation, or influence assimilation, and together account for more than 60 % of explained variance. Although minority_resistance is not the strongest driver of mean yes-vote share, it acts as the principal buffer against runaway conformity at the extremes of the parameter space, confirming the theoretical minority influence mechanism. The subsequent local analysis focuses exclusively on these three parameters: trust_adjustment_rate (ψ), info_decay_rate (λ), learning_rate (μbase), since they are the only three with an importance score greater than 0.2.

Running mean diagnostics indicated relative drift below 5 % after the fourth replication for every parameter-value pair, satisfying the convergence criterion. Non-parametric bootstrap resampling (n = 30) then produced narrow 95 % confidence intervals (width ≤0.04) around adoption means, and robustness scores (computed as 1−σ/μ, where σ and μ are the standard deviation and mean of adoption outcomes across the 30 bootstrap resamples for the same parameter setting) exceeded 0.97 for all focal parameters, indicating that these effect estimates are highly stable across stochastic variations.
Table 7 summarizes the one-at-a-time parameter sweeps, reporting both absolute and normalized effect sizes (normalized effect = Δ adoption/Δ parameter):
The normalized effect sizes provide a standardized measure of parameter influence that accounts for different parameter ranges, facilitating direct comparison of response sensitivities.

These findings confirm that stochastic elements do not obscure systematic parameter effects. Normalized effect sizes derived from the One-at-a-Time sweeps revealed that learning_rate produced the largest positive change in adoption, info_decay_rate produced a moderate negative change, and trust_adjustment_rate exerted a smaller positive influence, all with robustness scores above 0.97. The sensitivity workflow, therefore, achieves stable effect estimates within a tractable computational budget.

This section presents the simulation results, framed not as a simple comparison of policy interventions, but as a demonstration of the model's capacity to function as a policy sandbox. The model serves to dissect the complex, non-linear dynamics of collective action, revealing the mechanisms through which information campaigns translate into community-level outcomes. This section first establishes baseline dynamics by analyzing the model's sensitivity to core variables before introducing more scenarios.

The model simulates 40 households arranged on a Watts-Strogatz small-world graph (8 initial neighbors, 0.2 rewiring probability). This number was chosen to be large enough to observe complex network effects and community formation, yet small enough to be computationally tractable and representative of a small, cohesive decision-making unit, such as a Dutch VvE (usually less than 50 houses) [49], where collective heating decisions are often made. Initial attitudes are drawn from a normal distribution; Each agent's initial continuous opinion is generated as a weighted composite of its economic, environmental, and comfort attitudes plus a small term for system-replacement urgency, with Gaussian noise added and the result clipped to the [0,1] range, so that stronger pro-transition attitudes translate into a higher initial support. In the information-injection experiments, either the economic or the environmental attitude is modified as a one-time boost or drop for the affected agents.

Three main levers during a community-level decision-making of heating adoption, information timing (when the message arrived), targeting strategy (who received the new message first), and message valence (what message), are tested in this model. These three drivers form a 2 × 2 × 2 design space; the analysis focuses on four representative combinations that disentangle their main effects while keeping total simulation runs, as shown in Table 8. The selected magnitudes for these interventions (+0.20, +0.30, −0.40) are not intended as precise empirical estimates but as representations of significant informational shocks. All attitude and opinion variables are on a normalized scale from −1.0 to +1.0, where +1.0 represents unwavering support for the transition, and −1.0 represents intractable opposition. The selected magnitudes for information shocks are therefore illustrative values situated within this bounded range. A +0.20 attitude shift can be conceptualized as the effect of a targeted information campaign highlighting a favorable engineering report, while a −0.40 shock represents a negative event, such as a news story about technical failures in a similar project. Different observers might quantify the impact of such events differently; therefore, the analysis focuses on the directional dynamics and relative impacts rather than claiming predictive precision for these specific values.

In scenarios involving targeted information, the recipients (“leaders”) were selected through a process designed to mimic real-world engagement strategies. At each community detection interval, the Louvain algorithm partitioned the network into its emergent social clusters, and top agents were designated as leaders for subsequent information injections (see Section 3.4). This method was chosen to simulate a strategy of targeting influential ‘community champions’ who are central to their respective social circles. This choice profoundly influences information diffusion by concentrating influence within homophilous clusters, thereby enabling a direct examination of the tension between intra-group opinion consolidation and inter-group outreach, a dynamic explored further in Section 5.4 Discussion. In random-seed scenarios, an equivalent number of households were drawn uniformly at random to serve as the initial information recipients. Two message schedules are modeled: Early (rounds 10 & 15, i.e., just after neighbors have exchanged first impressions in the meeting) and Late (rounds 120 & 125, i.e., last-time opinion exchange right before the final vote).

Before running the scenarios,the network generation was validated to ensure the small-world network was constructed correctly and that community leaders were identified successfully. Fig. 5 depicts the small-world network after community detection for Scenario 1, revealing five topological communities (colors) and one nominated leader per community (squares).

This network has an average clustering coefficient of 0.36; a value ≥ 0.3 indicates the tight local cliques. The average path length (2.06) measures the average social “handshakes” needed for any household to reach another; values ensure information can jump across blocks without becoming globally homogeneous. Therefore, the validation proceeded by verifying small-world characteristics: (i) observed high clustering alongside short average path length, and (ii) visual community structure with plausible leaders from the Louvain + composite-centrality pipeline. This step is because network topology is a precondition for the bounded-confidence and social-pressure mechanisms; in line with the small-worlds being appropriate for communities, this paper additionally tests topology robustness across scale-free and random networks in Section 5.3.
Scenario 1 - early leader-centered positive campaign
Fig. 6 visualizes opinion evolution during Scenario 1 and how average opinion and adoption rate respond to early leader-centered positive information.

An economic boost at round 10 increased the seeded leaders’ mean economic attitude from 0.674 to 0.774, and an environmental boost at round 15 raised their environmental concern from 0.450 to 0.613. Within approximately 30 rounds, these shifts propagated through the network, moving most neighbors into the supportive region: evidence that targeted messages to influential nodes efficiently shift community opinion under bounded confidence and social pressure mechanisms (Section 2).

Communities 0, 1, and 3 converged to narrow opinion bands (σ<0.13), meaning that almost all opinions lie within ±0.13 of the community mean: an indicator of strong internal consensus. Adoption exceeded two-thirds in these groups, whereas Community 4 stalled at 20 % because its self-focused leader processed the boost weakly.

Adopting results in different styles (Fig. 7) show unanimous adoption among imitation and repetition agents, whereas deliberative and social comparison agents adopted at a lower rate, raising final polarization to 0.213 despite high average support.
Scenario 2 - early information, random seeds

When the same positive payloads were assigned to random seeds, diffusion rose to near-universal adoption (0.97) (see Fig. 8). The resulting polarization is 0.203. This outcome, which notably exceeds the leader-targeted benchmark (S1), is an emergent property of the network topology and trust dynamics, as analyzed in Section 5.4.
Scenario 3 - early negative information via leaders

A −0.4 economic shock and −0.3 environmental shock (numerically, a 0.40 loss in economic attitudes and a 0.30 drop in perceived environmental attitudes, both attitudes are on a 0-to-1 scale) introduced at rounds 10 and 15 reversed the trajectory (see Fig. 9). 90 % of agents' intentions fell below the 0.1 stopping threshold by round 30, triggering an early-stopping mechanism and terminating the simulation (if the injected negative information is minor, like −0.1, it would not activate the early-stopping mechanism. Over time as the information diffuses, its negative impact may fade and agents may gradually regain the intention). This rapid collapse of support is not a numerical artifact but an emergent finding: the shock pushes the leaders’ opinions so far from the community mean that they fall outside the confidence bounds of many neighbors, effectively severing positive influence pathways. Simultaneously, the potent negative signal quickly flips the local majority opinion, triggering a powerful conformity cascade toward rejection. This aligns with the principles of prospect theory and empirical findings on loss aversion and negativity bias, underscoring that preventing or neutralizing negative narratives is a critical policy challenge [60–62]. The early termination represents a collective disengagement, a scenario where the discourse becomes so negative that a significant portion of the community withdraws from the decision-making process entirely.
Scenario 4 - late-stage leader campaign

Positive messages delivered shortly before voting (rounds 120 and 125) yielded a high final adoption (95 %) with only a modest opinion shift (+0.05), see Fig. 10; many fence-sitters were near threshold, and fresh cues from respected leaders tipped their decisions. Deliberative agents showed the strongest response (all approval for adoption), whereas imitation agents registered 0.75 owing to limited propagation time.
Table 9 summarizes outcomes across scenarios, highlighting contrasts in adoption rate, opinion change, polarization, and consensus.

Community structure still governs how signals translate into votes, but the targeting advantage is not universal. In four scenarios, random early seeding achieved higher final adoption (97 %) than leader-targeted early seeding (88 %). This outcome challenges the conventional assumption that seeding central influencers is always the optimal strategy for information diffusion. The result is not an anomaly but rather an emergent property of the model's specific mechanics, particularly the interplay between how leaders are identified within homophilous communities and how trust-weighted social pressure governs influence. A full mechanistic dissection of this phenomenon, which underscores the critical distinction between embedded bonding leaders and boundary-spanning bridging actors, is provided in the Discussion (Section 5.4). Differences in polarization were modest (S4 = 0.212 vs. S2 = 0.203 vs. S1 = 0.213), suggesting that under positive framing, both early and late breadth support higher uptake without introducing additional polarization.

The timing-valence interaction remains decisive. The late leader push (S4) produced 95 % adoption with only ∼+0.05 opinion movement, confirming that late cues maximize conversions per unit of opinion change by nudging near-threshold agents. Conversely, early negative framing (S3) zeroed adoption and triggered early stop, reflecting the reality: when people heard significant negative news, they might leave discussions immediately and abstain from voting. Style-wise, imitation and repetition again acted as accelerants of whichever signal dominated; deliberative agents reached full adoption under late credible cues, while social-comparison agents lagged when local majorities were ambiguous.

To balance generalizability with mechanistic transparency, this section reports replication-averaged outcomes for each scenario and uses a single representative run to visualize trajectories (Figs. 6–10). Holding the network seed fixed in those trajectory plots enables clear causal tracing of how an intervention propagates through trust, bounded confidence, and intention accumulation.

To address concerns about the generalizability of findings beyond small-world network structures, a systematic comparative analysis across three distinct network topologies is conducted. Three network are tested: small-world (Watts-Strogatz with initial 4 neighbors, 20 % rewiring probability), scale-free [63] (Barabási-Albert with 4 edges attached per new node), and random [64] (Erdős-Rényi with 10 % connection probability) networks; under identical simulation conditions, maintaining agent populations (n=40), decision-making style distributions, and information injection parameters (economic +0.2, environmental +0.3 at rounds 10 and 15). These parameter choices ensured comparable edge densities (9.5–10.3 %) across network types while preserving their distinctive topological characteristics. Each network type was generated with controlled seeds to ensure reproducibility.

The three network types displayed markedly different topological properties while maintaining comparable densities (9.5–10.3 %). Small-world networks exhibited moderate clustering (0.260) with longer average path lengths (2.995). Scale-free networks showed the highest clustering coefficient (0.292) and shortest path lengths (2.369). Random networks displayed the lowest clustering (0.106) with intermediate path lengths (2.877).

Across topologies, collective outcomes differed in magnitude. Under the same positive early injection, scale-free networks achieved the highest adoption rate (82.5 %), followed by random networks (77.5 %) and small-world networks (75.0 %). The superior performance of scale-free networks can be attributed to their hub-dominated structure, where highly connected agents serve as efficient information broadcasters.

Network structure also moderated the effectiveness of leadership-targeted information campaigns. The leadership advantage is the difference in final yes votes between simulations seeded via leaders vs. the same-number random nodes. The leadership advantage was largest in the scale-free topology (+7.5 percentage points), moderate in the small-world topology (+5.0 percentage points), and negligible or slightly negative in the random topology (−2.5 percentage points).

Overall, the topology comparison indicates that the model's outcomes are sensitive to network structure in predictable ways (both in absolute yes-vote share and in the size of any leader-targeting advantage), while still producing qualitatively similar diffusion-and-consensus dynamics across all three network classes. The next section interprets how these structural differences relate to the mechanisms highlighted in the scenarios.

Current ABM research on community energy systems can be synthesized into three domains, from recent systematic reviews [16,65–67]: (1) technology diffusion [68]; (2) economic and market mechanisms, particularly peer-to-peer electricity trading [69]; and (3) institutional design and governance [56,70]. However, prior models seldom combine collective-choice rules and micro-level social-psychological opinion change within a single framework, especially in the context of thermal energy communities; moreover, much of the ABM literature centers on electricity rather than heat networks.

To address the gaps, this model focuses on a collective thermal energy decision (district heating), which involves different socio-technical challenges, such as indivisible infrastructure and the need for super-majority consent, than the individual adoption of heat pump, etc. Specifically, this model fills a gap between abstract opinion dynamics models and applied technology adoption models. Instead of assuming a decision-making framework or modeling influence as an abstract network effect, this model explicitly simulates the messy, iterative, pre-decisional process of opinion formation and consensus building. The methodology choice is deliberate: standard adoption ABMs capture independent uptake but under-represent pre-vote opinion cascades; discrete-choice/econometric approaches estimate average effects but typically assume weak interdependence; and system-dynamics models aggregate away who-influences-whom, limiting the evaluation of when and where to intervene (often used at the macro level) [71].

Community-level structure and message design are two pivots that determine whether a neighborhood-scale heat transition stalls or scales. First, on-the-fly community detection does more than tidy up the social graph: it exposes the mechanism through which average support or global consensus can conceal pockets of resistance or early enthusiasm. By partitioning the network into Louvain communities, the model could re-assign variance from global statistics to between-community processes; Scenario 1 illustrated this when three communities converged while one remained skeptical at 20 % adoption, a pattern invisible to aggregate polarization metrics.

The S2 result (97 % adoption), exceeding S1 (88 %), is influenced by the specific random seed used (seed 42); however, it is consistent with three mechanisms embedded in the implementation: First, leaders are identified within each detected community using a convex combination of degree, betweenness, and eigenvector centralities (10 % per community). This tends to select highly embedded nodes at the core of homophilous clusters rather than boundary spanners. “Leaders” are often echo-chamber anchors rather than cross-cutting brokers. Thus, early injections to leaders (S1) mainly intensify already-leaning pockets while leaving hesitant peripheries under-reached. Second, initial edge trust is built from multi-attribute similarity and then boosted within neighborhoods (up to 0.9), and social pressure uses a trust-weighted neighbor majority. This design amplifies within-bloc reinforcement but does little to privilege paths that cross low-trust boundaries. When seeds are random, more trust “islands” light up in parallel; when seeds are leaders, influence concentrates within their already cohesive islands.

This model's leader definition privileges embeddedness, not bridging. For interventions intended to cross boundaries, targeting trust-bridging nodes (e.g., high edge-betweenness or high “bridging trust” between dissimilar neighborhoods) would likely dominate leaders-only strategies. Another implication is that in the current diffusion routine, information decays by distance but not by path credibility. Incorporating a path-trust factor (e.g., geometric mean trust along the shortest path) would make trust an explicit gate for message travel and may reduce over-concentration in already cohesive clusters.

Besides, given the asymmetric treatment of negative information (stronger and longer-lasting), early detection and counter-messaging remain essential. The trust-weighted pressure channel makes local downturns steep; containment should prioritize high-trust cores before they tip neighbors. This model should be viewed not as a source of prescriptive answers, but as a tool to sharpen strategic thinking about the social dynamics that underpin collective energy transition.

Applying insights from the results requires working within the existing institutional tools and constraints of the Dutch heat transition. The model's finding that positive economic framing can tip fence-sitters, for instance, provides a direct rationale for the strategic promotion of instruments like the Nationaal Warmtefonds (National Heat Fund). This fund, which offers 0 % interest loans to households with incomes below €60,000, is a targeted financial incentive that can shift the cost-benefit calculus for deliberative agents; an effective communication strategy would therefore be a targeted campaign making eligible households aware of this specific instrument rather than a generic message about affordability. Similarly, the collective decision process simulated in the model is institutionalized through Wijkuitvoeringsplan (District Implementation Plan, WUP), the formal arenas for the deliberation and voting that the model simulates. The model's results suggest that a WUP's success is critically dependent on the socio-dynamic processes within its participatory framework. In this context, abstract concepts can be translated into concrete actions: social topology can be approximated by leveraging proxies like VvE board structures or municipal energy workshop participation, and a recommendation to target credible brokers translates into empowering figures like neighborhood energy coaches during the WUP consultation phase.

Several limitations require future work. First, the opinion metric conflates multiple motives; separating cost-benefit evaluation, risk perception, and environmental concern could expose interaction effects, for example, where high perceived risk overrides social proof. Second, and most critically, the model is not empirically calibrated or validated. The input data is synthetic, and its parameters (as in Table 4) are illustrative and based on theoretical plausibility, not empirical data. A validation that only matches macro-outcomes (e.g., final yes-vote share/adoption rate) would be insufficient. A meaningful validation must address the processing of the decision-making mechanisms themselves. This would necessitate calibrating the social-psychological mechanisms, for example, the empirical value for the bounded confidence threshold in a Dutch VvE meeting, or the strength of the conformity coefficient. This requires novel, longitudinal empirical data, such as opinion-tracking and network mapping derived from real-world Wijkuitvoeringsplan (WUP) deliberations, to capture the process of consensus itself, not just the final vote.

Third, leader identification emphasizes embeddedness and may underweight boundary-spanning brokers; future work should test bridging-aware metrics (e.g., participation coefficient). Fourth, the early-stopping rule for negative shocks simplifies real deliberation and may overstate withdrawal; adding institutional safeguards (e.g., second-chance meetings) would be informative. Furthermore, the model is conceptualized based on the Dutch context, and its applicability to countries with different housing stocks, energy policies, or cultural norms around collective decision-making would require significant adaptation. Finally, leader identification could be augmented with bridging-aware criteria (e.g., community-based betweenness, participation coefficient), and the diffusion kernel could be extended to trust-on-path to test whether S2's advantage persists once credible cross-community routes are explicitly rewarded.

The Netherlands has committed to phasing out natural-gas boilers by 2050, and the district heating grid fed by aqua thermal, geothermal, or industrial waste-heat sources is a preferred choice. Installing such a shared system is not a household-level purchase but a collective action on pipes under the street and a long-term supply contract.

This paper used district heating as a use case, where the three-layer agent-based model situates decision-making where it actually happens, such as housing association meetings, places, where economic pay-offs, comfort expectations, environmental norms, and replacement urgency are weighed against each other. Four empirically grounded cognitive styles (deliberative, social comparison, repetition, imitation) translate these attitudes into continuous opinions, then into intentions, and finally into a “yes/no” vote on whether to sign the district-heating contract.

Three communication levers (who receives information first, when they receive it, and how it is framed) jointly determine the final voting results. The results suggest that who is seeded matters less than how many trust clusters are activated early (S1: 88 % yes-vote share compared to S2: 97 %). Random early seeding worked not because leaders are unimportant, but because it incidentally covered more clusters and styles under a trust-weighted social-pressure dynamic. In practice, one should complement ‘leaders-first’ programs with trust-bridging seeding and style-aware outreach, treating trust not only as a channel amplifier but as a design variable that dictates where messages can, and cannot, spread. The style-specific adoption rates suggest segmenting outreach: provide data-rich, comparative pay-off calculators for deliberative homeowners; visible early-adopter stories for social-comparison types; and hands-on demonstrations for imitators and habitual users.

The practical application of these insights requires operating under the existing institutional arrangements and restrictions of the Dutch heat transition. Social topology can be approximated not by exhaustive mapping but by leveraging proxies such as VvE board structures, participation records from municipal energy workshops, or the networks of local energy coaches. Credible brokers often align with existing roles (e.g., those energy coaches, sustainability advisors), though budgetary and volunteer constraints must be considered. Similarly, the need for rapid counter-communication against negative narratives requires municipalities and energy cooperatives to prepare predefined response templates rather than relying on ad hoc messaging. These steps do not eliminate uncertainty, but they demonstrate how the model-derived heuristics can be translated into feasible interventions within the limits of current practice, making tools like the financing from the Nationaal Warmtefonds more effective on the ground.

By integrating bounded confidence, social-impact theory, minority influence, dual-process cognition, and dynamic information diffusion into one ABM, this study advances the computational modeling of socio-technical transitions. It provides a novel model that connects the micro-dynamics of opinion formation, often studied in isolation, to the macro-level outcomes of technology adoption, a key concern for energy systems modelers. It thus serves as a bridge between abstract opinion dynamics models and more descriptive, case-based energy transition studies. In addition, it provides a set of strategic heuristics to inform the design of engagement campaigns for the heat transition. Policymakers gain a sandbox to test “what-if” outreach strategies before spending political capital. This paper also offers a modular framework for researchers that can be ported to other collective-choice problems.

In conclusion, this paper makes several distinct contributions to theory, method, and policy practice:•
Methodological & Theoretical: This study introduces a novel three-layer agent architecture (opinion-intention-vote) that bridges the gap between abstract opinion dynamics models and applied technology adoption models, providing a new framework for studying collective action problems where continuous deliberation leads to a discrete, binding choice. Theoretically, the results demonstrate that in systems governed by bounded confidence and social pressure, the topology of trust is paramount. The distinction between embedded “bonding” leaders and boundary-spanning “bridging” actors is a critical determinant of diffusion success, challenging simplistic influencer-first strategies.•
Policy Heuristic: Engagement strategies should be diversified. Complement targeting of central community figures (88 % yes-vote share in S1) with outreach to bridging individuals who connect disparate social clusters to avoid reinforcing echo chambers and accelerate network-wide consensus (97 % in S2); The timing and valence of information are critical non-economic levers. Early, potent negative narratives can be fatal to a project and must be proactively neutralized. Late-stage, positive messaging is highly efficient for converting undecided fence-sitters just before a decision point (95 % in S4).

Future work should tackle empirical validation by calibrating the model against multi-year neighborhood adoption data and by surveying residents. Nonetheless, the core insight stands: successful heat transitions require as much social engineering as pipe-laying, and both can be planned with the same socio-computational lens.
